title: The pressure is growing to get SNAP payments right
summary: USDA’s FY 2025 SNAP data tells a striking story: a 10.62% national payment error rate and $10.1B in improper payments. As the stakes rise for states, payment accuracy needs to start earlier.
body_text: As SNAP payment error rates become tied to state funding, states need earlier ways to find and prevent avoidable errors. For years, SNAP’s payment error rate was mostly a measure of administrative hygiene. The metric shows whether state agencies were determining eligibility correctly, calculating benefits accurately, and fixing weaknesses through appropriate means. But what was once a compliance metric is quickly becoming a fiscal liability. As federal policy links error rates more directly to state funding responsibility, accuracy is moving from the program integrity office to the budget table. Earlier this year, USDA reported that the national SNAP payment error rate for fiscal year 2025 was 10.62%, well above the 6% congressional threshold. The figure represents $10.1 billion in improper payments, including both overpayments and underpayments. USDA also noted that H.R. 1, the federal budget reconciliation law enacted in 2025, creates new financial consequences for states with high SNAP error rates. States at or above the 6% threshold may have to pay part of their SNAP benefit costs. Depending on the error rate, that state share could be 5%, 10% or 15%, beginning in most cases on Oct. 1, 2027. For state agencies, the practical effect couldn’t be more straightforward: SNAP accuracy is becoming a budget liability. Related: Brochure: Reduce SNAP payment errors and protect federal funding Why SNAP accuracy is difficult to manage SNAP administration is complex by design. States must determine eligibility, calculate benefits, verify household information, manage renewals and respond to changes, all while maintaining timely access for eligible residents. USDA’s quality control process measures whether households received the correct benefit amount and includes both underpayments and overpayments. For state leaders, the challenge goes beyond identifying errors after they occur. States now need enough visibility into the eligibility process to prevent avoidable errors before benefits are authorized. Better data at intake reduces downstream errors Payment accuracy begins well before a caseworker ever makes a determination. Missing documents and incomplete income information can all create risk later in the process, making intake one of the most important places to prevent errors. When applicants are guided to submit complete, accurate information, agencies can reduce follow-up work and provide caseworkers with a stronger record for making decisions. Real-time validation helps caseworkers act with confidence SNAP eligibility decisions often depend on information from multiple systems. When those systems are disconnected, caseworkers may have to reconcile data manually, increasing the chance of missed details or inconsistent decisions. By flagging missing, conflicting or unusual information before a case moves forward, agencies can give staff clearer information at the point of decision and reduce errors before they become part of the payment record. Continuous monitoring gives states earlier warning signs Federal error rates are reported after the fact, meaning the underlying issues may have been building for months before states see the full picture. Continuous monitoring gives agencies a more current view of where risk is emerging. Dashboards, trend reporting and risk scoring can help leaders identify patterns earlier, focus on review of higher-risk cases and make targeted operational adjustments before small issues become larger findings. How Conduent helps states strengthen SNAP payment accuracy Our teams help agencies embed validation, analytics and digital self-service into the eligibility process. VeriSight AI-Powered Eligibility Solution supports eligibility teams with analytics that help detect fraud, identity theft and eligibility risks, while helping staff focus attention on higher-risk cases. AI that supports SNAP payment accuracy By analyzing information across systems, VeriSight can flag cases that may need additional review and help caseworkers focus attention where it matters most. The goal is to give eligibility teams better visibility into missing, conflicting or unusual information at the point of decision. For state leaders, VeriSight also supports continuous monitoring by helping agencies track trends, identify emerging risk patterns and improve program accuracy before issues become formal findings. Together, these capabilities can help agencies reduce manual processing errors, improve consistency across case decisions and identify payment accuracy trends before they become audit findings. Just as important, they support accuracy without creating unnecessary barriers for eligible residents. Making SNAP program accuracy part of every step The new SNAP accountability environment raises the stakes for states. But it also clarifies the path forward: make program accuracy part of every step, from application to verification to authorization to recertification to reporting. By building accuracy into the eligibility process, states can protect funding, support compliance, and continue delivering timely access to the people who rely on SNAP. title: IDEAYA Biosciences Announces Inducement Grants under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4)
summary: IDEAYA Biosciences, Inc. (NASDAQ: IDYA), a precision medicine oncology company committed to the discovery and development of targeted therapeutics, today announced that, on July 30, 2026, the...
body_text: SOUTH SAN FRANCISCO, Calif. , July 31, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- IDEAYA Biosciences, Inc. (NASDAQ: IDYA), a precision medicine oncology company committed to the discovery and development of targeted therapeutics, today announced that, on July 30, 2026, the Compensation Committee of IDEAYA's Board of Directors granted non-qualified stock options to purchase an aggregate of 260,200 shares of the Company's common stock to fourteen newly hired employees. The stock options were granted under the IDEAYA Biosciences, Inc. 2023 Employment Inducement Incentive Award Plan (2023 Inducement Plan) as an inducement material to such individuals' entering into employment with IDEAYA in accordance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4). The 2023 Inducement Plan is used exclusively for the grant of equity awards to individuals who were not previously employees of IDEAYA, or following a bona fide period of non-employment, as an inducement material to such individuals' entering into employment with IDEAYA, pursuant to Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4). The stock options have an exercise price of $36.40 per share, which is equal to the closing price of IDEAYA's common stock on The Nasdaq Global Select Market on the date of grant. The stock options have a 10-year term and will vest over four years, with 25% of the options vesting on the first anniversary of the vesting commencement date and the remaining 75% of the options vesting in equal monthly installments over the three years thereafter. Vesting of the stock options is subject to such employee's continued service to IDEAYA on each vesting date. About IDEAYA Biosciences IDEAYA is a precision medicine oncology company committed to the discovery, development, and commercialization of transformative therapies for cancer. Our approach integrates expertise in small-molecule drug discovery, structural biology and bioinformatics with robust internal capabilities in identifying and validating translational biomarkers to develop tailored, potentially first-in-class targeted therapies aligned to the genetic drivers of disease. We have built a deep pipeline of product candidates focused on synthetic lethality and antibody-drug conjugates, or ADCs, for molecularly defined solid tumor indications. Our mission is to bring forth the next wave of precision oncology therapies that are more selective, more effective, and deeply personalized with the goal of altering the course of disease and improving clinical outcomes for patients with cancer. title: The Ecommerce Sourcing Guide: 7 Steps To Build a Resilient Supply Chain
summary: This 7-step sourcing guide walks you through everything from supplier vetting and diversification to the growing role of AI in procurement.
body_text: For many ecommerce businesses, sourcing starts as a simple search for the lowest price. But as brands grow, that approach gets harder to sustain. Rising costs, supply chain disruptions , shifting customer expectations, and increasing competition all put pressure on sourcing decisions. In an episode of the Unboxing Logistics podcast , host Lori Boyer sat down with Mattia Miglio of Alibaba.com to discuss how sourcing is evolving and what businesses can do to build stronger supplier strategies. We’ve turned their conversation into a seven-step guide that walks you through everything from supplier vetting and diversification to the growing role of AI in procurement. It all starts with understanding your business’s pricing, positioning, costs, and customers. Step 1: Understand your competitive position Many businesses look for sourcing opportunities without first understanding how their costs compare to the rest of the market. But in order to effectively evaluate suppliers, you need to understand where your business stands in relation to the competition. To gain this understanding, Mattia recommended conducting a competitive analysis Specifically, compare: Product pricing Production costs Shipping and logistics costs Product positioning Customer expectations This creates a benchmark that helps you determine whether your current sourcing model is still competitive. Without that context, it’s hard to know whether rising costs are a supplier problem or simply a reflection of broader market conditions. A few extra tips … Look beyond manufacturing costs One common mistake when choosing suppliers is focusing only on unit cost. The cheapest supplier isn’t always the most cost-effective one once transportation, lead times, quality issues, and operational complexity enter the equation. As Lori pointed out, supply chains have become increasingly complex and difficult to navigate. Understanding the full cost of getting a product into customers’ hands often matters more than shaving a few cents off manufacturing costs. Make competitive analysis an ongoing process Sourcing isn’t a one-time decision. Mattia recommends regularly comparing your products, suppliers, and costs against the broader market. Even if you’re happy with your current supplier relationships, keeping an eye on alternatives ensures you aren’t missing new opportunities. Step 2: Vet suppliers carefully These days, finding suppliers is easier than ever. Finding reliable suppliers? Not so much. Fortunately, there’s a simple solution: conduct supplier assessments. Whether you’re sourcing through an online marketplace, attending trade shows, or working through referrals, keep the evaluation consistent across the board. What to look for Before moving forward with a supplier, consider: Business verification Customer reviews Years in operation Manufacturing capabilities Certifications Research and development capacity With so many areas to delve into, this assessment will take some time. But don’t rush! Thoroughly exploring each of these categories will give you a comprehensive picture of a supplier’s legitimacy and reliability. Warning signs When evaluating suppliers, keep an eye out for the following red flags: Few or no reviews Limited operating history Missing certifications Unclear communication Pricing that seems dramatically lower than competitors Bottom line? If something feels too good to be true, it’s worth taking a closer look. Step 3: Focus on relationships, not transactions One of Mattia’s key takeaways was that strong supplier relationships can create advantages that go far beyond pricing. In fact, he prefers to steer clear of the term supplier altogether, focusing more on the mutual benefits of a partnership. “I always recommend [finding] the right partner , not a supplier.” Reliable partners are often more flexible during inventory shortages, production delays, or peak season demand spikes. They also have a deeper understanding of your products and long-term business goals. Step 4: Start small Even if a supplier looks great on paper, Mattia cautioned against moving too quickly. Before committing significant volume to a new supplier, consider following these steps: Request samples Evaluate quality Verify certifications Place a small initial order Step one is especially important. When Lori asked about balancing quality control with speed to market, Mattia’s answer was immediate: “Never, never, never bypass [the product sample stage].” Testing product quality early can help prevent expensive mistakes later, especially when launching new products or working with unfamiliar suppliers. Step 5: Diversify your supplier network Many businesses still rely heavily on a single supplier. While that strategy may work during stable periods, recent years have shown how quickly conditions can change. So even if you have a trusted supplier relationship, keeping alternatives on hand can provide valuable insurance. Mattia recommended: Keeping backup suppliers available Monitoring emerging suppliers Evaluating regional alternatives Comparing pricing regularly He also reminded listeners that supplier diversification isn’t only about quantity—it’s also about geography. He noted that many businesses are exploring suppliers closer to their customers while maintaining their global sourcing relationships. These balanced networks can help reduce shipping costs, shorten lead times, and create contingency options when disruptions strike. Step 6: Use AI to source smarter One of the most interesting parts of the conversation focused on the growing role of artificial intelligence in sourcing. Historically, supplier discovery required extensive research, manual comparisons, and significant procurement expertise. Today, AI is beginning to simplify many of those tasks. As Mattia explained, “AI is revolutionizing how businesses are doing ecommerce, and especially B2B ecommerce.” Where AI can help today Modern sourcing tools can help with: Supplier discovery Product research Request for quotation (RFQ) creation Quote comparisons Market analysis Product concept development For smaller businesses without dedicated procurement teams, these capabilities help level the playing field. AI doesn’t replace judgment Despite its advantages, AI isn’t a substitute for supplier relationships, product testing, or strategic decision-making. Instead, it’s a tool that helps you evaluate more options in less time. The final decisions still require human judgment. Step 7: Keep improving your sourcing strategy Businesses that periodically review their sourcing approach are often better positioned to adapt when conditions change. Mattia recommended continuing to compare and monitor suppliers, explore new technologies, and attend industry events to stay up-to-date with market trends. Even if you don’t switch suppliers, understanding your options gives you leverage and flexibility. Building a sourcing strategy that lasts Supply chains have become more complex, but they don’t have to become more chaotic. The businesses best positioned for long-term success aren’t necessarily the ones with the lowest costs. They’re the ones that understand their market, build strong supplier relationships, diversify risk, and continuously look for ways to improve. Whether you’re sourcing products locally, globally, or somewhere in between, the goal remains the same: create a supply chain that’s dependable enough to support growth and flexible enough to handle change. For additional insights from Lori and Mattia, be sure to watch the full podcast recording . title: Understanding Fluidic Fitting Threads: A Practical Guide
summary: Threaded fittings play a critical role in system integrity and performance. Yet, identifying and understanding fitting threads is often overlooked.
body_text: When working with fluidic systems in life science applications—whether in chromatography, diagnostics, or analytical instrumentation—threaded fittings play a critical role in system integrity and performance. Yet, identifying and understanding fitting threads is often overlooked until an issue arises. This guide walks you through how to identify fitting threads, understand thread standards, and ensure proper selection for reliable fluidic connections. What Do Fitting Thread Callouts Mean? Most fluidic fittings use standardized thread callouts that provide key information about their geometry. Typically, a thread designation includes two numbers: Diameter (e.g., 1/4): Indicates the maximum outer diameter of the threaded portion Thread pitch (e.g., 28): Specifies the number of threads per inch For example: 1/4-28 means the fitting has a 1/4-inch diameter and 28 threads per inch (TPI) . Understanding this designation is the first step in selecting compatible components and avoiding leaks, dead volume, or failures in your system caused by fittings. Why Thread Identification Matters In fluid handling systems, mismatches between threads can result in: Leaks or pressure loss Damaged ports or fittings Compromised analytical results Identifying threads in fittings is essential to maintaining system performance. How to Measure English (Imperial) Threads You can often determine thread type with simple tools—a ruler and careful observation. Step 1: Count Threads Over a Known Distance Align the threaded section of the fitting with a ruler Measure across a 1/4-inch section Count the number of threads within that distance Important: The first thread is your zero point. Do not include it in your count. Multiply the number of threads within 1/4 inch by four to calculate threads per inch. Example: 7 threads in 1/4 inch → 28 threads per inch → 1/4-28 thread Step 2: Measure Thread Diameter Place the fitting against a ruler and measure across the widest point of the threads. This gives you the nominal diameter. Together, these two measurements define the fitting’s thread specification. Common Thread Patterns in Chromatography In many chromatography systems, thread diameter and pitch often follow consistent pairings. While exceptions exist, these patterns provide a helpful starting point when identifying fittings. For example: Smaller diameters typically correlate with finer thread pitches Larger diameters may have fewer threads per inch Using known industry standards can help narrow down possibilities before confirming measurements. Understanding Metric Threads Metric-threaded fittings are increasingly common in modern fluidic systems. They follow a different convention than imperial threads. A typical metric designation looks like: M6 x 1 This indicates: M6 → 6 mm thread diameter 1 → 1 mm distance between threads (pitch) Key Difference: English threads: threads per inch Metric threads: distance between threads How to Measure Metric Threads The process is similar but uses millimeter measurements: Step 1: Determine Thread Pitch Align the fitting with a metric ruler Match a thread crest with a millimeter mark Observe spacing between threads For common metric fittings, each thread crest will align consistently with millimeter increments (e.g., 1 mm spacing for M6 x 1). Some fittings may follow different spacing patterns (e.g., 0.7 mm pitch), so look for repeating intervals. Step 2: Measure Diameter Measure across the widest part of the threads using the metric scale to determine nominal diameter. Simplifying Thread Identification If manual measurement isn’t practical, visual identification tools can help: Thread silhouette charts for quick comparison Printed guides to match fitting profiles Reference diagrams to verify measurements Overlaying your fitting against known shapes can quickly confirm thread size and type, reducing trial-and-error during setup. Download and Print this Thread Measurement Chart at 100% Best Practices for Reliable Connections To ensure optimal system performance: Always verify both thread size and type (metric vs. imperial) Avoid forcing mismatched threads Use compatible fittings and components from trusted suppliers Double-check specifications when replacing legacy components Supporting Precision in Fluidic Systems Thread identification may seem like a small detail, but it has a significant impact on the accuracy, reliability, and longevity of life science instrumentation. By understanding thread standards and applying simple measurement techniques, you can confidently select fittings that maintain system integrity, supporting consistent, high-quality results across your workflows. title: Natural Gas Utility Workers’ Day: A Message from Melody Birmingham
summary: Today, I want to recognize our natural gas employees. The people who show up every day to serve their communities and keep energy flowing safely.
body_text: Today, I want to recognize our natural gas employees. The people who show up every day to serve their communities and keep energy flowing safely. Because of you, families can heat their homes and businesses can open their doors. That kind of reliability doesn’t happen by accident. It comes from preparation, discipline and looking out for one another, often in tough conditions and without much recognition. Safety isn’t a slogan here. It’s a responsibility you carry every day. I see it in the way you maintain our systems, respond when customers need us, and take seriously the trust placed in you. Your work also helps keep energy reliable and affordable for the people who count on us, especially when it matters most. Thank you to our natural gas teams across Columbia Gas and NIPSCO, and to our partners, for the pride and professionalism you bring to this work. Melody Birmingham Executive Vice President and Group President Utilities NiSource Inc. Hear more from our Executive Vice President and Chief Operating and Safety Officer, Bill Jefferson

title: Animal Welfare Certification vs. On-Farm Audits: Clearing Up the Confusion
summary: When it comes to animal welfare, consumers are increasingly looking for assurance that the products they purchase come from farms that prioritize humane treatment of animals. body_text: When it comes to animal welfare, consumers are increasingly looking for assurance that the products they purchase come from farms that prioritize humane treatment of animals. However, confusion often arises between the concepts of animal welfare certification and the actual on-farm audits. While both are essential components of ensuring animal welfare, they are distinct processes that serve different purposes. Animal welfare labels can be confusing—especially when terms like audit and certification are used interchangeably. They’re related, but not the same. What Is an Animal Welfare Audit? An audit is the evaluation process . It assesses: Animal health Living conditions Feeding practices Handling methods Caretaker training Documentation and Record-keeping Etc. Audits are conducted by trained third-party auditors. The purpose of an animal welfare audit is to identify areas for improvement and ensure compliance with an established welfare standard. What Is Animal Welfare Certification? Certification is the outcome . It confirms that a farm has met defined standards and allows them to use a verified label. Animal welfare certification is a formal recognition that a farm meets specific standards related to the humane treatment of animals. When a certification is earned that means it is following guidelines and regulations set forth by that specific certification standard. It typically will result in a status or label that can be displayed on productsand by the farm itself. Certification signifies that a farm has undergone a thorough evaluation process and has demonstrated adherence to established animal welfare criteria. Key Characteristics of Animal Welfare Certification Standards-Based: Certification programs are based on specific, predefined standards that must be met to obtain certification. Program-Driven: Various organizations and initiatives create certification programs tailored to different livestock species and production practices. Results in Label or Status: Once certified, farms can use the certification label on their products, providing consumers with assurance about their animal welfare practices. Key Differences Between Certification and Audits To help clarify the distinctions between animal welfare audits and certification, let's break down the key differences in the table below: Aspect Audit Certification Definition Process of evaluating practices Formal recognition of meeting specific standards Purpose To assess compliance and identify areas of improvement To provide a label or status indicatingadherence to standards Frequency Conducted Regularly (e.g., annually, quarterly, bi-annually, etc) Granted after successful completion and review of an audit Outcome Report with findings and recommendations Certification status and label for products Conducted By Third-party Auditors Certification Body, Final Review of Auditor Findings Nature Ongoing Process Final Designation How They Work Together Audits = the mechanism Certification = the result No audit → no certification How Audits Support Certification Audits are the actual mechanism through which animal welfare certification is achieved. An audit evaluates a farm’s practices against the established standards set by the certification program. Here’s how the two processes interact: Audits = Mechanism: Audits provide the necessary assessment to determine whether a farm meets the required standards for certification. Typically, in many instances and in many animal welfare standards, this requires as onsite audit, which for animal welfare is very important since the welfare of the animal should be observed in person to truly assess whether a farm deserves to receive that certification. Consumers need to do their research of the animal welfare label they are seeking trust out of to ensure it aligns with their values – and if an onsite evaluation is something they value. Certification = Outcome: Once a farm successfully completes an audit and meets the criteria, it is awarded certification, allowing the use of the certification label. In essence, audits serve as the foundation for certification, ensuring that only farms that adhere to high animal welfare standards earn the right to display the certification label. What Happens During an On-Farm Audit? During an on-farm audit, you can expect auditors to conduct a thorough inspection of the farm's operations. The process typically includes: Pre-Audit Preparation: Farms prepare by reviewing their records and practices in advance of the audit. Onsite Walk-Through: Auditors perform a walk-through of the facilities, observing animal living conditions and handling practices. Record Review: Auditors examine records related to animal health, nutrition, and care practices to ensure compliance with standards. Interviews: Auditors may interview farm personnel to assess their understanding of animal welfare practices and any procedures the farm claims to have in place. Reporting: After the audit, auditors compile a report detailing their findings and any necessary corrective actions. The goal of an on-farm audit is to ensure that all aspects of animal welfare are being addressed and to provide feedback for improvement. Why Both Matter for Animal Welfare Claims Both animal welfare audits and certifications are crucial for substantiating claims related to animal welfare. Here’s why: Consumer Confidence: Certification allows brands to communicate their commitment to animal welfare, building trust with consumers who prioritize humane treatment. Continuous Improvement: Regular audits help farms identify areas for improvement, ensuring that animal welfare standards are continually met and enhanced. This is crucial when looking to improve both the agriculture and food industry landscapes. Transparency: Audits provide an objective assessment of animal welfare practices, offering transparency to consumers and stakeholders. In summary, both audits and certifications play vital roles in promoting animal welfare and ensuring that claims made by producers are backed by rigorous evaluation and standards. It is up to consumers to determine if the labels they are actively supporting and trusting are backed by a third-party verified standard. Common Misconceptions Despite the clarity provided here, several misconceptions persist regarding animal welfare audits and certification: “Audit = Certified” False. Audits assess. Certification approves. “One audit is enough” False. Ongoing audits are required to maintain certification. Bottom Line Audits and certification are two parts of the same system. Together, they ensure that animal welfare claims are not just stated but verified.
